corpus_definition: to make the sounds of a word using your mouth and voice.

forms.definition: the way in which a word or a language is said
forms.example: Her English pronunciation is very clear.
forms.note: Spelling trap: pronounce, but pronunciation (no 'o' after 'n').

syn.note: Related: an accent is the way a group of people speak, for example a Scottish accent.
Related and formal: how clearly you make each sound.
Related: how your voice goes up and down when you speak.

ant.note: A wrong way of saying a word.

forms.definition: an official public statement about something important
forms.example: The president made a pronouncement about the new law.
forms.note: Belongs to pronounce = say something officially ("I now pronounce you husband and wife"), not saying the sounds of a word.

forms.definition: to make the sounds of a word with your mouth
forms.example: How do you pronounce your surname?

syn.note: Easy everyday word: "How do you say this word?"
Formal: to say sounds or words clearly.
Formal: to say each sound very clearly and carefully.
Related: speak is general; pronounce is about the sounds of one word.

ant.note: To say a word in the wrong way.

forms.definition: very easy to notice
forms.example: He walks with a pronounced limp.
forms.note: Belongs to a different meaning (strong and noticeable), not saying the sounds of a word.
No common adverb in this family.

context.text: Our English teacher in Tashkent helps us pronounce difficult words. She says clear pronunciation is more important than a perfect accent.

reviewer_note: Spelling trap pronounce/pronunciation handled; pronounced (noticeable) and pronouncement (official statement) are other_meaning; mis- forms kept as antonyms.

corpus_definition: a short, well-known saying that gives wise advice

forms.definition: a short, well-known sentence that gives wise advice
forms.example: There is an Uzbek proverb about patience.

syn.note: Easy everyday word with the same meaning.
Formal: an old saying that many people believe is true.
Formal: a short rule about how to behave.
Related: any group of words with a special meaning; it does not always give advice.
Related: a short sentence that a person, school or company chooses to live by.

forms.note: No verb in this family.

forms.definition: well known, like the words of a famous old saying
forms.example: Finding him in the crowd was like looking for the proverbial needle in a haystack.

syn.note: Related: known by many people.
Related: very famous and talked about a lot.

forms.definition: as people say in a well-known old saying
forms.example: Time, proverbially, is money.

syn.note: Related: in a way that many people know about.

context.text: My grandmother knows a proverb for every situation. When I complain, she gives me her proverbial advice: patience turns into gold.

reviewer_note: proverbial often means 'the famous phrase' (the proverbial needle); kept as existing in this meaning.

corpus_definition: a large region or area that is part of a country

forms.definition: one of the large areas that some countries are divided into
forms.example: Canada has ten provinces.
forms.note: 'The provinces' means all the parts of a country outside the capital.

syn.note: Very close; in Uzbekistan a viloyat is usually called a region in English.
Related: the name for a big part of countries like the USA or India.
Related: a smaller area, often part of a province or city.
Related: land that belongs to a country or ruler.

forms.note: No verb in this family.

forms.definition: connected with one of the large areas of a country
forms.example: The provincial government built a new hospital.
forms.note: It can also mean 'from outside the capital', and sometimes 'old-fashioned', which is not polite.

syn.note: Very close: connected with a region.
Related: connected with the place where you live, often smaller.
Related: connected with the countryside, not towns.

ant.note: Connected with a very big city or the capital.

forms.note: No common adverb in this family.

context.text: Samarkand is a city and also the name of a province in Uzbekistan. Every year many students from provincial towns move to Tashkent to study.

reviewer_note: Uzbekistan's viloyat is usually 'region' in English; noted on the synonym.

corpus_definition: Buses and trains that anyone can use.
usage_note: Uncountable: 'use / take public transport', 'go by public transport' (no 'a'). American English usually says public transportation.

relations.note: The same thing in American English.
Mainly American and more formal, used in news and planning.
Related: any way of moving people or things, including cars.
Your own car or bike, not shared buses and trains.

context.text: In Tashkent, public transport is cheap and the metro is very fast. I go to university by public transport every day.

reviewer_note: Fixed noun phrase; British/American difference noted.

corpus_definition: to prepare and produce a book or magazine for people to buy.

forms.definition: the act of printing a book or magazine and offering it for sale
forms.example: The publication of her first novel made her famous.
forms.note: It can also mean the book or magazine itself: 'a weekly publication'.

syn.note: Related: making a book, film or song available to people.
Related: making copies on paper; it is only one part of the work.
Related: one copy of a magazine or newspaper that comes out on a date.

forms.definition: to print a book or magazine and offer it for sale
forms.example: She wants to publish her new book next year.
forms.note: Also used for putting a text online: 'publish a blog post'.

syn.note: Phrasal verb, a little informal: "They brought out a new edition."
Easy word; print is about making copies on paper.
Related: used more for films, songs and products.
Related: to put a message or photo on the internet.

forms.definition: printed and available for people to buy and read
forms.example: This is his first published article.

syn.note: Close; printed is only about paper copies.

ant.note: Written but not yet printed or offered to the public.

forms.note: No adverb in this family.

people.definition: a person or company that prepares and sells books or magazines
people.example: The publisher sent her a contract for two books.

people.definition: the business of preparing and selling books and magazines
people.example: My aunt has worked in publishing for twenty years.

context.text: My cousin wrote a book of Uzbek stories, and a company in Tashkent agreed to publish it. Since its publication last year, the published book has sold well.

reviewer_note: publication/public: no -ation affix claimed because removing it leaves 'public', not the base verb.

corpus_definition: A soft, sweet dessert served after a meal.

forms.definition: a soft sweet food eaten at the end of a meal
forms.example: We ate chocolate pudding for dessert.
forms.note: In British English it can mean any dessert ('What's for pudding?'). Some British puddings are not sweet, like Yorkshire pudding.

syn.note: Any sweet food at the end of a meal; pudding is often soft.
British English noun for dessert: "What's for sweet?"
Related: a sweet yellow sauce or soft food made with milk and eggs.

forms.note: No verb in this family.
No adjective in this family.
No adverb in this family.

context.text: After plov, my host family in London served rice pudding. I liked the pudding so much that I asked for the recipe.

reviewer_note: British sense 'any dessert' and savoury puddings mentioned in a note only.

corpus_definition: the regular beat of the heart felt in the body

forms.definition: the regular beat of blood that you can feel at your wrist or neck
forms.example: The doctor checked the patient's pulse carefully.
forms.note: Different word: pulses (plural) are also beans and lentils as food.

syn.note: Very close; heartbeat is the movement of the heart itself.
The number of beats in one minute; used by doctors and sports watches.
Related: one regular sound or movement, of a heart or of music.
Related: a regular repeated pattern of sounds or movements.

forms.definition: to move or flow with strong regular beats
forms.example: She could feel the blood pulsing through her body.

syn.note: Easy word: "My heart was beating fast."
To beat strongly, often with pain: "My head was throbbing."
Related: to beat very hard and loud, often from fear or exercise.

forms.definition: to move in and out with strong regular beats
forms.example: The music pulsated through the whole building.

forms.definition: very exciting and full of energy
forms.example: It was a pulsating match from start to finish.
forms.note: Belongs to the meaning 'exciting', used about games and music, not the beat you feel in your wrist.
No adverb in this family.

context.text: After running in the park, Aziz checked his pulse. He could still feel the blood pulsing in his neck five minutes later.

reviewer_note: pulses (beans and lentils) is a different word, only mentioned in a note; pulsating 'exciting' is other_meaning.

corpus_definition: to make someone suffer because they did something bad or wrong

forms.definition: something bad that is done to a person who broke a rule
forms.example: His punishment was to stay after school.

syn.note: Often an official punishment, like a fine or a penalty in football.
Related: training people to follow rules, sometimes with punishment.
Related: the punishment a judge gives in a court.

ant.note: Something good you get because you did something well.

forms.definition: to make someone suffer because they did something wrong
forms.example: The teacher had to punish the noisy student.

syn.note: Used about parents, schools and companies correcting bad behaviour.
More formal, often for breaking official rules. British spelling: penalise.
Related: to punish someone by making them pay money.

ant.note: To give someone something good for doing well.
To stop being angry and not punish someone.

forms.definition: that can be dealt with by a court or by law
forms.example: Stealing is a crime punishable by prison.

syn.note: Related: against the law; punishable says there is a legal penalty.

forms.definition: very hard and making you very tired
forms.example: The team trains on a punishing schedule.
forms.note: Belongs to the meaning 'very difficult and tiring', not making someone suffer for doing wrong.

forms.definition: in a way that is extremely hard or tiring
forms.example: The climb up the mountain was punishingly steep.
forms.note: Goes with punishing = very hard and tiring, not making someone suffer for doing wrong.

context.text: My little brother broke a window, but my parents didn't punish him. His only punishment was to help clean the yard.

reviewer_note: punishing/punishingly (very hard) kept as other_meaning; punitive left out as a formal C1+ word.

corpus_definition: The main goal or reason for doing something.

forms.definition: the reason why you do something or why something exists
forms.example: What is the purpose of this meeting?
forms.note: Phrase: on purpose = not by accident.

syn.note: Easy word with almost the same meaning.
Easy word; a goal is often something you work towards for a long time.
Reason answers 'why?'; purpose answers 'what for?'.
What you plan to do; a little more formal.
Formal, used in business and education.
Informal: "What's the point of doing this?"

forms.note: The verb is old-fashioned and not used by learners.

forms.definition: having a clear aim and showing that you know what you want
forms.example: She walked to the front with purposeful steps.

syn.note: Close: you will not let anything stop you.
Related: giving all your attention to one aim.
Related: important and useful.

ant.note: Without a clear aim or plan.

forms.definition: in a way that is planned and not by accident
forms.example: I purposely left my phone at home.

syn.note: Easy and common in speaking.
Same meaning, very common.
Same meaning, a little more formal.

forms.definition: in a determined way, with a clear aim
forms.example: He walked purposefully towards the door.

context.text: The purpose of my trip to Bukhara was to visit my grandparents. I purposely left my laptop at home, and I spent each day in a calm, purposeful way.

reviewer_note: purposely (deliberately) vs purposefully (in a determined way) shown as separate adverbs; archaic verb set to no_form.

corpus_definition: to follow or try hard to achieve something

forms.definition: the act of trying hard to get or achieve something
forms.example: Many young people move to the city in pursuit of a better job.
forms.note: Plural pursuits also means hobbies: 'outdoor pursuits'.

syn.note: Related: trying to find something.
Related: running after someone or something.
Related and literary: a long, hard search for something.

forms.definition: to try hard to achieve something over a long time
forms.example: She decided to pursue a career in medicine.
forms.note: Also means to chase someone: 'The police pursued the car.'

syn.note: Easy word: "follow your dreams", "follow a career".
Formal: to try to find or get something.
Related: to run after someone; informal for goals: "chase your dreams".
Related: to try to reach a goal.

ant.note: To stop trying to do something.
To stop doing a plan completely, often because it is too hard.

forms.note: No common adjective in this family.
No adverb in this family.

people.definition: a person who is following or chasing someone
people.example: The thief ran faster and escaped from his pursuers.

context.text: After school, Dilnoza wants to pursue a career in medicine. Her pursuit of this dream means long evenings of study, but she never complains.

reviewer_note: Corpus sense covers both 'follow' and 'try to achieve'; pursuer kept as existing person.
